# CS 29.917 — Design (rotor drive system)

> [!summary]
> CS 29.917 defines the rotor drive system of a large rotorcraft, requires a
> design assessment of it, and sets six arrangement rules. It is a CS-29
> specification, not a CS-E one, and the rotorcraft applicant owns it. The
> definition brings the gearbox lubricating systems and the oil coolers inside
> the rotor drive system. The design assessment is what the loss-of-lubrication
> test of CS 29.927(c) rests on. The paragraph is about twice the length of its
> CS-27 counterpart, and the difference is substantive.

## Requirement

The verbs below are CS-29's own. They bind the rotorcraft applicant, not the
engine applicant. See `## Bearing on this engine` for what reaches CS-E.

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **(a)** | General. The rotor drive system includes any part necessary to transmit power from the engines to the rotor hubs: gearboxes, shafting, universal joints, couplings, rotor brake assemblies, clutches, supporting bearings for shafting, any attendant accessory pads or drives, lubricating systems for drive system gearboxes, oil coolers and any cooling fans that are a part of, attached to, or mounted on the rotor drive system. | Statement |
| **(b)** | Perform a design assessment to ensure that the rotor drive system functions safely over the full range of conditions for which certification is sought. | Required |
| **(b)** | Include in the design assessment a detailed failure analysis identifying all failures that will prevent continued safe flight or safe landing, and identify the means to minimise the likelihood of their occurrence. | Required |
| **(c)** | Arrangement. Sub-points (c)(1) to (c)(6) set how rotor drive systems must be arranged. | Statement |
| **(c)(1)** | Arrange each rotor drive system of a multi-engine rotorcraft so that each rotor necessary for operation and control will continue to be driven by the remaining engines if any engine fails. | Required |
| **(c)(2)** | For a single-engine rotorcraft, arrange each rotor drive system so that each rotor necessary for control in autorotation will continue to be driven by the main rotors after disengagement of the engine from the main and auxiliary rotors. | Required |
| **(c)(3)** | Incorporate in each rotor drive system a unit for each engine to automatically disengage that engine from the main and auxiliary rotors if that engine fails. | Required |
| **(c)(4)** | Locate a torque limiting device, where one is used in the rotor drive system, so as to allow continued control of the rotorcraft when the device is operating. | Required |
| **(c)(5)** | Where the rotors must be phased for intermeshing, provide a constant and positive phase relationship under any operating condition. | Required |
| **(c)(6)** | Where a rotor dephasing device is incorporated, provide means to keep the rotors locked in proper phase before operation. | Required |

Sub-point (a) imposes no action, and it is not decoration either. It fixes what
(b) and (c) are about, and it is where CS-29 and CS-27 first part company:
CS 29.917(a) names "lubricating systems for drive system gearboxes, oil coolers"
among the parts of the rotor drive system [ext CS 29.917(a)], and CS 27.917(d)
does not [ext CS 27.917(d)].

Sub-point (b) is the sub-point with no CS-27 counterpart and the one that
carries the most weight. It asks that "A design assessment must be performed to
ensure that the rotor drive system functions safely over the full range of
conditions for which certification is sought" [ext CS 29.917(b)]. The failure
analysis it requires is what CS 29.927(c) draws its simulated failure mode from
[ext CS 29.927(c)], and AMC2 29.917 below is its acceptable means. The test
itself is recorded in [[CS 29.927]] and is not repeated here.

Sub-points (c)(1) and (c)(2) divide by engine count, so only one of them applies
to any one rotorcraft. CS-27 draws no such division: its autorotation rule is
unqualified, and it has nothing corresponding to (c)(1), (c)(5) or (c)(6). The
comparison is set out in [[CS 27.917]].

### Acceptable means — AMC2 29.917, lubrication systems

AMC2 29.917 supplements FAA Advisory Circular AC 29-2C, § AC 29.917(b), and
should be used in conjunction with that AC. It sets out the applicant's
dedicated safety assessment of the lubrication systems of the rotor drive system
gearboxes, and how that assessment is used to comply with CS 29.927(c)
[ext AMC2 29.917]. Its sub-point labels below are the AMC's own.

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **(a)** | Identify any single failure, malfunction, or reasonably conceivable combination of failures that may result in a loss of oil pressure, a loss of oil supply to the dynamic components or a loss of the oil scavenge function. This normally takes the form of a failure mode and effects analysis. | Accepted method |
| **(a)** | Identify compensating provisions to minimise the likelihood of occurrence of those failures, and consider potential assembly or maintenance errors that cannot be readily detected during specified functional checks. | Accepted method |
| **(b)** | Consider any specific design features that are subject to variability in manufacture or to wear or degradation in service and that could have an appreciable effect on the maximum period of operation following loss of lubrication. Take any feature that may significantly influence the behaviour of the residual oil or of the auxiliary lubrication system into account when determining the configuration of test articles. | Accepted method |
| **(c)** | Identify the most severe failure mode, that is the one giving the shortest duration for which the gearbox should be able to operate after the flight crew is told of a normal-use lubrication system failure, and use it to simulate lubrication failure during the loss-of-lubrication test of CS 29.927(c). | Accepted method |
| **(d)** | Where compliance with CS 29.927(c) relies on an auxiliary lubrication system, substantiate sufficient independence between the normal-use and the auxiliary lubrication systems, and perform common-cause failure analysis including common-mode, particular-risk and zonal safety analyses. | Accepted method |
| **(d)** | Establish that no single failure or identified common-cause failure will prevent the operation of both the normal-use and the auxiliary lubrication systems, apart from any failure determined to be an extremely remote lubrication failure. Consider also the effects of inadvertent operation of the auxiliary lubrication system. | Accepted method |
| **(e)(1)** | Lubrication system failure: in the context of CS 29.917(b), a failure of the lubrication system is any failure that results in a loss of pressure and an associated low oil pressure warning, within the duration of one flight. | Statement |
| **(e)(2)** | Most severe failure mode: the failure mode of the normal-use lubrication system that results in the shortest duration of time in which the gearbox is expected to operate following an indication to the flight crew. | Statement |
| **(e)(3)** | Normal-use lubrication system: the lubrication system relied upon during normal operation. | Statement |
| **(e)(4)** | Auxiliary lubrication system: any lubrication system that is independent of the normal-use lubrication system. | Statement |
| **(e)(5)** | Independent: an auxiliary lubrication system should be able to function after a failure of the normal-use lubrication system. Show failure modes that may cause the subsequent failure of both systems and may prevent continued safe flight or safe landing to be extremely remote lubrication failures. | Accepted method |
| **(e)(6)** | Extremely remote lubrication failure: a lubrication failure whose likelihood of occurrence has been minimised, either by structural analysis in accordance with CS 29.571 or by laboratory testing. In-service experience or other means may be used instead, indicating a level of reliability comparable with one failure per 10 million hours. | Statement |
| **(e)(6)** | Do not treat failure modes including failures of external pipes, fittings, coolers or hoses, or any component that requires periodic removal by maintainers, as extremely remote lubrication failures. | Accepted method |
| **(f)(1)** | Conduct a careful analysis of the potential failure modes, taking the effects of flight conditions into account where relevant. The most severe failure mode may not be immediately obvious, because leakage rates vary and system performance after leaks from different areas varies as well. | Accepted method |
| **(f)(2)** | Start from an assessment of all the potential lubrication system failure modes, as part of the CS 29.917(b) design assessment, including leaks from any connection between components that are assembled together, such as threaded connections, hydraulic inserts, gaskets, seals and packing (O-rings). | Accepted method |
| **(f)(2)** | Consider also failure modes such as failures of external lines, failures of component retention hardware, and wall-through cracks that have not been substantiated for CS 29.307, CS 29.571 and CS 29.923(m). Substantiate any determination that a failure is an extremely remote lubrication failure where that determination eliminates a candidate most severe failure mode. | Accepted method |
| **(f)(2)** | Conduct a laboratory test where leakage rates or the effect of failure modes cannot be easily determined. Once the most severe failure mode is determined, make it the basis of the conditions for the start of the test. | Accepted method |
| **(g)** | The use of an auxiliary lubrication system may be an acceptable means of providing extended operating time after a loss of lubrication. | Permitted |
| **(g)** | Conceive the design so that shared components and interfaces between the normal-use and the auxiliary lubrication systems are minimised and comply with the design assessment provisions of CS 29.917(b). Show that a failure of any common feature that could fail both systems, and would reduce the maximum period of operation following loss of lubrication, is an extremely remote lubrication failure. | Accepted method |
| **(g)(1)** | Where compliance with CS 29.927(c) relies on an auxiliary lubrication system, perform additional loss of lubrication tests simulating a combined failure of both systems, to substantiate additional RFM emergency procedures for that failure. Those procedures should instruct the flight crew to LAND IMMEDIATELY unless the additional tests justify an increased duration. | Accepted method |
| **(g)(2)** | Provide a means of verifying that the auxiliary lubrication system is functioning properly during normal operation of the rotorcraft, on a periodic, pre-flight or continual basis, and alert the flight crew to any malfunction after a failure of the normal-use system has activated the auxiliary system. | Accepted method |
| **(h)(1)(i)** | A failure of any pressurised portion of the normal-use lubrication system should not result in a subsequent failure of the auxiliary lubrication system. | Accepted method |
| **(h)(1)(ii)** | Show common failure modes that defeat both systems to be extremely remote lubrication failures, unless testing conducted to comply with CS 29.927(c) demonstrates that the failure mode does not compromise the maximum period of operation following loss of lubrication. | Accepted method |
| **(h)(1)(iii)** | Do not share control systems, logic and health-reporting systems, and give consideration in the design process to appropriate segregation of the control and warning systems in the system architecture. | Accepted method |
| **(h)(2)** | Demonstrate that failure modes of common areas are extremely remote by field experience of the exact design with an exact application; field experience with a similar design or application, with supporting test data allowing a comparison; demonstration by test of extremely low leakage rates; redundancy of design; structural substantiation with a high safety margin for elements of the lubrication systems assessed against CS 29.571; or assessment of the potential dormant failure modes of the auxiliary lubrication system, determining its health before each flight to minimise the risk of dormant failures. | Accepted method |

The AMC is an acceptable means, so its "should" is labelled Accepted method
throughout. Sub-point (g) is the exception that reads as a permission: an
auxiliary lubrication system "may be an acceptable means of providing extended
operating time after a loss of lubrication" [ext AMC2 29.917]. Nothing obliges
the applicant to fit one; the rest of (g) and all of (h) apply once one is
credited.

The definitions in (e) are the vocabulary the loss-of-lubrication test uses.
Two of them fix a test condition rather than describe one. A lubrication system
failure is "any failure that results in a loss of pressure and an associated
low oil pressure warning, within the duration of one flight"
[ext AMC2 29.917(e)(1)], which is what starts the clock. An extremely remote
lubrication failure needs "a level of reliability comparable with one failure
per 10 million hours"
[ext AMC2 29.917(e)(6)], which is what lets a candidate failure mode be set
aside.

CS-29 publishes three AMCs for point 917. Only AMC2 29.917 is sliced into
`work/external/`, and only its content is stated above. `AMC1 29.917` and
`AMC3 29.917` exist — [[CS 27.927]] records all three — and this vault
does not hold them.

[VERIFY: what AMC1 29.917 and AMC3 29.917 require. Neither is sliced into
`work/external/`, so the vault cannot state their content, and neither is
written from memory. Adding them means adding them to WANTED in
`scripts/external_paragraphs.py`.]

## Bearing on this engine

CS 29.917 creates no CS-E obligation. The rotor drive system is not part of the
engine type design, and the design assessment is the rotorcraft applicant's.
Three of its interfaces are fed by engine data.

**Lubrication.** Sub-point (a) puts the gearbox lubricating systems and the oil
coolers inside the rotor drive system [ext CS 29.917(a)]. That is where the
boundary is drawn: the gearbox lubrication system belongs to the rotorcraft, and
the engine Oil System of [[CS-E 570]] is a different system with its own
evidence. The low oil pressure warning defined in AMC2 29.917(e)(1) is the
gearbox's warning, not the engine's. The test that runs from it is recorded in
[[CS 29.927]].

**Torque limiting devices.** Sub-point (c)(4) requires a torque limiting device,
where one is used, to be located so as to allow continued control of the
rotorcraft when it operates [ext CS 29.917(c)(4)]. Where that limiting function
sits in the full authority EECS declared in `engine_profile.md`, the device is
inside the engine type design: its integrity is engine-side evidence under
[[CS-E 50]], and its failure behaviour reaches the safety analysis of
[[CS-E 510]].

[VERIFY: whether the EECS torque limiting function is the torque limiting device
of CS 29.917(c)(4), or whether a separate device sits in the transmission.
`engine_profile.md` declares a full authority EECS and does not say where the
torque limit is set. The answer decides whether (c)(4) reads on engine data at
all.]

**Data the installer needs.** The design assessment of (b) must identify all
failures that will prevent continued safe flight or safe landing
[ext CS 29.917(b)]. Where such a failure is an engine failure, or a failure of
the engine control system acting through the drive, the engine applicant
supplies the failure conditions and their effects through [[CS-E 510]], and the
installation instructions required by [[CS-E 20]] are the route to the
installer. The automatic disengagement unit of (c)(3) acts on engine failure and
draws on the same two sources.

**Arrangement.** Sub-point (c)(1) requires each rotor necessary for operation
and control to continue to be driven by the remaining engines if any engine
fails [ext CS 29.917(c)(1)]. `engine_profile.md` declares a multi-engine
installation, so (c)(1) is the applicable arrangement rule and (c)(2) is not. It
is the design premise behind the OEI ratings declared under [[CS-E 40]]: the
power the remaining engines deliver is a CS-E declaration, and the arrangement
that carries it to the rotors is CS-29's.

Sub-points (c)(5) and (c)(6) consume no engine data. They govern the phase
relationship of intermeshing rotors and the locking of a rotor dephasing device,
and neither reads on the engine.

The airframe code is not fixed. [[CS-E 30]] carries that open item, and the
difference between the two codes at point 917 is set out in [[CS 27.917]].
